1372|"That's not the committee's call," she says. "This one's mine."
1373|
1374|She thinks about the truss, the sail, the pods. She thinks about the laser beam that will push this impossible structure out of Earth orbit and into the dark. She thinks about the crew who will wake in a hundred and twenty years and look out a window at a star that is not their sun, and they will need to know that someone went first, that someone proved the path was passable, that the distance was not too great and the fragility was not too fatal and the math worked after all.
1375|
1376|"Pathfinder," she says. "Ship 1 is Pathfinder."
1377|
1378|She closes the channel. She floats in the silence of the integration bay and looks at the ship she has named, and the ship does not look back, and she does not expect it to. She has twenty-eight more to go. The work continues.
1379|# Chapter 15: Saboteur Hunt
1380|
1381|![](chapter_images/ch12.png)
1382|
1383|James Kovacs has been staring at the same personnel file for twenty minutes, and the file is telling him nothing.
1384|
1385|The file belongs to a technician named David Mensah, age thirty-one, assigned to Platform 6's environmental systems division. Mensah accessed Platform 7's Deck 4 at 0130 on the night of the canister rupture — thirty minutes before the pressure valve was opened. His access was logged, his badge was scanned, his presence was confirmed by the bay's internal camera. He was there. He says he was checking an air filtration unit on the adjacent wall, which is plausible, because the filtration unit was due for maintenance and Mensah's work order confirms the assignment. He says he did not go near Canister 4-C, which is plausible, because the camera shows him on the far side of the bay, and the valve is on the near side. He says he did not see anyone else, which is not plausible, because the camera shows Yuki Tanaka entering the bay at 0145, and Mensah's line of sight to the entrance is unobstructed.
1386|
1387|Kovacs makes a note: *Mensah claims he did not see Tanaka. Camera shows otherwise. Discrepancy. Follow up.*
1388|
1389|He closes the file and opens the next one. Forty-three people had access to Platform 7's Deck 4 in the seventy-two hours before the canister rupture. Forty-three people who could have opened the manual valve, who could have overpressurized the nitrogen supply, who could have killed four workers and destroyed enough sail membrane for four ships. Kovacs has been working through the list for six days. He has cleared twenty-two. He has flagged nine. He has referred three to Mark Reeves, the security chief for the orbital construction program, for deeper investigation.
1390|
1391|Reeves is in the next room — a storage closet on Platform 1 that Kovacs's team converted into a secure office by bolting a desk to the floor and installing a communication terminal with an encrypted uplink. The door is open. Kovacs can see Reeves at the desk, his face lit by the blue glow of his terminal, reading files with the methodical patience of a man who has spent twenty years in military intelligence and has learned that the truth is never in the first layer of any document.
1392|
1393|"Mark."
1394|
1395|Reeves looks up. He is fifty-three years old, former British Army, recruited by the Lightship program eighteen months ago to build a security architecture for an orbital construction project that did not exist six months before that. He has the build of a man who was once very strong and is now merely solid, and the eyes of a person who has read too many files containing too many lies.
1396|
1397|"I've got a discrepancy on Mensah," Kovacs says. "He says he didn't see Tanaka in the bay. Camera shows he should have."
1398|
1399|Reeves pulls up the camera footage on his terminal. They watch it together — a grainy, high-contrast image of a man in a flight suit working on a filtration unit, his back to the bay entrance, while a woman in a different-colored suit enters through the hatch and walks to the far wall. The timestamp reads 0145:03. Mensah does not turn around.
1400|
1401|"He's focused on the filtration unit," Reeves says. "Could be he genuinely didn't notice."
1402|
1403|"Could be."
1404|
1405|"But you don't think so."
1406|
1407|Kovacs leans against the doorframe. He has not slept in thirty-one hours. His body is running on the particular fuel that exhaustion produces — a chemical cocktail of cortisol and adrenaline that keeps the mind sharp and the emotions flat, a state he has learned to recognize as useful but unsustainable. "I think Mensah is lying about something. I don't know if it's about the valve. I don't know if it's about Tanaka. I know the camera doesn't support his statement."
1408|
1409|Reeves makes a note. "I'll bring him in. Separately from Tanaka — we don't want them coordinating stories if there's a story to coordinate."
1410|
1411|"There isn't a story. Mensah was doing maintenance. Tanaka was doing an inspection. The valve was opened at 0200 by someone who wasn't on camera because the camera on the near wall of Deck 4 has been malfunctioning for three weeks."
1412|
1413|Reeves looks at him. "Malfunctioning how?"
1414|
1415|"Intermittent. The image drops out for periods of thirty seconds to two minutes. The maintenance log shows a repair request filed two weeks ago. The repair was scheduled for next month."
1416|
1417|"Convenient."
1418|
1419|"Everything about this is convenient. The camera malfunction. The pressure alarm cleared by one of the dead workers. The valve opened during a shift change when the bay was nominally unoccupied. If this was an accident, it was the most carefully timed accident in the history of orbital construction."
1420|
1421|Reeves closes the terminal. "You're certain it wasn't an accident."
1422|
1423|Kovacs is quiet for four seconds. Then: "No. I'm not certain. I'm certain that the evidence is consistent with sabotage. I'm certain that the evidence is also consistent with a catastrophic chain of human error. I am not certain which one it is, and that uncertainty is the thing that keeps me running at six miles a day on a treadmill in a space station while the world below freezes."
1424|
1425|He pushes off the doorframe and pulls himself back to his workstation. The next file on the list is Jennifer Wu.
1426|
1427|He has been avoiding this file. He knows this. Reeves knows this. The file sits at the bottom of his queue like a stone at the bottom of a river — everything else has moved past it, but it remains, and eventually he will have to pick it up.
1428|
1429|He opens it.
1430|
1431|Jennifer Wu, age twenty-nine. Fabrication specialist, Platform 5, Clean Room 3. Assigned to the Lightship program nineteen months ago. Performance reviews: exemplary. Security clearance: Level 3, granted after standard background check. No flagged communications prior to the encrypted network contact in Chapter 13. One flagged communication after: the message to Thomas Voss's Earth First network, intercepted by Kovacs's monitoring system, the one that said *I want to help.*
1432|
1433|Kovacs reads the file again. The background check is clean. Her parents are dead — father from pancreatic cancer at fifty-eight, mother from the influenza outbreak in Week 6 of the eruption. One sibling: Marcus Wu, Candidate 8,834, rejected from the colonist pool due to Pres1 mutation. 1434|
1435|Jennifer Wu has attended three psychological evaluations in nineteen months. All three are rated satisfactory. The evaluating psychologist notes that Wu demonstrates "appropriate coping mechanisms" and "a strong identification with the mission's objectives." The psychologist does not note — because the psychologist does not know — that Jennifer Wu sent a message to an Earth First network asking how she could help them stop the mission she is building.
1436|
1437|Kovacs pulls up the Earth First watchlist. It contains 1,247 names — people who have attended rallies, posted manifestos, signed petitions, or been identified by intelligence services as members or sympathizers of the movement that believes the Lightship program is an abomination, that the resources spent on the ships should be directed toward saving the people on Earth, that the selection process is eugenics dressed in the language of genetics, and that the ships should never launch.
1438|
1439|Marcus Wu is not on the list. Jennifer Wu is not on the list. Thomas Voss is on the list — flagged as a regional coordinator for the São Paulo cell, known to organize meetings in the industrial district, suspected of coordinating with sympathizers in the orbital construction workforce. The suspected orbital sympathizers are not named. The intelligence is thin — based on intercepted communications that reference "someone on Platform 5" without identifying details.
1440|
1441|Someone on Platform 5. Jennifer Wu works on Platform 5. Jennifer Wu sent a message to Thomas Voss's network. The message said *I want to help.* Jennifer Wu has access to Clean Room 3, which produces the sail membranes — the single most critical and irreplaceable component of every ship in the fleet.
1442|
1443|Kovacs closes the file. He opens a new channel — encrypted, routed through three relay nodes, accessible only to Reeves and himself.
1444|
1445|*Wu is on the access list for Deck 4. She was in the bay at 0145. She had fifteen minutes before the valve was opened. Her file is clean except for the encrypted contact, which we already know about. Her brother was rejected by the Selection Committee. She has motive. She has access. She has made contact with Earth First. But she was not near the valve. The camera shows her on the far side of the bay. And the valve was opened at 0200, fifteen minutes after the camera on the near wall went dark.*
1446|
1447|He sends the message. Reeves reads it and responds in forty seconds.
1448|
1449|*Agree she's a person of interest. But the camera gap is the problem. If the camera had been working, we'd know who was near the valve at 0200. Without it, we have a fifteen-minute window and no visual confirmation. Could be Wu. Could be Mensah. Could be someone else entirely who entered during the camera gap.*
1450|
1451|Kovacs stares at the message. He thinks about the first sabotage, the one that came from the ground, from someone who hacked a guidance system and sent eleven tonnes of freight into Platform 2. That saboteur was never identified. The investigation traced the signal to a ground-based transmitter near Alcântara, but the people who operated it were never found. Kovacs has a theory about that sabotage — that it was a test, a proof of concept, a demonstration that the orbital platforms were vulnerable. If he is right, then the canister rupture is not the second sabotage. It is the third. And the saboteur is still inside.
1452|
1453|He opens Jennifer Wu's file one more time. He reads the section on her brother. Marcus Wu, Candidate 8,834. Structural engineer. Pres1 mutation, homozygous. Predicted onset age fifty-three to fifty-eight. Rejected.
1454|
1455|Kovacs thinks about what it means to love someone the world has decided is not worth saving. He thinks about the rage that produces — not the hot rage of a moment, but the cold rage of months, the kind that builds like ice, layer by layer, until it is load-bearing, until it is the thing that holds you up. He has seen it before. He saw it in Yuki Tanaka's eyes during the interrogation. He has seen it in the messages his monitoring system intercepts from the ground — the Earth First communiqués, the manifestos, the desperate manifestos of people who are watching the planet die and cannot understand why the people with the resources to save them are building ships to leave.
1456|
1457|He does not believe Jennifer Wu opened the valve. He does not believe she did not open the valve. He believes the evidence is insufficient, and insufficient evidence is not the same as innocence, and the distinction matters when the stakes are thirty-six lives per ship and twenty-nine ships and a hundred and twenty years of transit and the entire future of a species that is running out of time on a planet that is running out of heat.
1458|
1459|He closes the file and moves to the next name on the list.
1460|
1461|---
1462|
1463|On Platform 5, Jennifer Wu is standing at the observation port of Clean Room 3, watching Layer 67 of Sail Assembly 34 spread across the deposition frame, when the message arrives.
1464|
1465|It comes through the encrypted network — the same network she contacted seven months ago, the same relay nodes, the same absence of sender identification. She reads it on her wrist display, her hands still inside her clean-suit gloves, her eyes still on the membrane.
1466|
1467|*Target the laser array calibration data. Small errors will tear the sails at full power. The array's targeting system relies on precision alignment values stored in the calibration database. Alter the values by zero point zero zero five arc seconds or less — small enough to pass automated verification, large enough to produce asymmetric thrust at full beam intensity. A sail under asymmetric thrust will oscillate. An oscillating sail will tear. A torn sail means a ship that does not arrive. This is not about stopping the launch. This is about ensuring that the ships that launch do not survive the transit. The people on those ships deserve to know that their journey ends in the dark. Make it happen.*
1468|
1469|Jennifer reads the message three times. She thinks about Marcus. She thinks about the Selection Committee members who are sleeping in training pods in Houston and Geneva, who voted to reject Candidate 8,834, who will wake in a hundred and twenty years on a world where Marcus's gene does not exist because Marcus was not allowed to carry it.
1470|
1471|She thinks about the sail she is watching — Layer 67 of 75, a membrane that will catch a laser beam and carry thirty-six people to the stars. She thinks about the calibration data, the alignment values, the zero-point-zero-zero-five-arc-second margin that separates a successful acceleration from a catastrophic tear.
1472|
1473|She thinks about the woman she is becoming — the woman who contacts Thomas Voss's network, the woman who reads instructions like these and does not immediately report them to Kovacs, the woman who stands at this window and watches polymer spread and feels the load-bearing structure inside her chest grow heavier with every layer.
1474|
1475|The spin-coater hums. The polymer spreads. Layer 67 is within tolerance.
1476|
1477|Jennifer saves the message to an encrypted partition on her wrist display. She does not delete it. She does not forward it. She opens the production log and begins calibrating for Layer 68.
1478|
1479|The work continues.
1480|# Chapter 16: The Colonist Uprising
1481|
1482|![](chapter_images/ch13.png)
1483|
1484|The work stoppage on Platform 3 begins not with a declaration but with silence.
1485|
1486|At 0600 on a Wednesday, forty-seven workers on Assembly Deck 7 do not begin their shifts. They remain in the docking gallery at the platform's midsection — a curved corridor with observation ports that face the construction bays — and they do not move. They do not speak into their radios. They do not acknowledge the shift supervisor's pages. They simply stand at the ports and look at the ships.
1487|
1488|David Okafor receives the call at 0611. He is in a transit capsule between Platform 1 and Platform 2, reviewing the sail deployment test schedule on his tablet, and the message from Platform 3's deck supervisor is four words: *We have a situation.*
1489|
1490|He reroutes the capsule.
1491|
1492|By the time he arrives at the docking gallery at 0634, the number has grown to sixty-one. Word spreads through the platform mesh network — an internal communication system that Okafor's team built for logistics and that the workers have repurposed into something closer to a strike coordination channel. He can see the activity on his wrist display: private channels multiplying, message volumes spiking, sixty-one people who were on shift schedules thirty minutes ago and are now something else.
1493|
1494|He enters the gallery and sees them clearly for the first time. They are riggers, welders, composite technicians, systems installers — the people who bolt the trusses together, who seal the sail canisters, who wire the hibernation modules to the systems bus. They are the hands that build the ships. Their faces are lit by the blue-white Earthlight that pours through the observation ports, and their expressions carry the particular flatness that Okafor recognizes from his years in labor negotiation: the look of people who have already decided.
1495|
1496|A woman steps forward. She is tall, broad-shouldered, with close-cropped hair and the calloused hands of a composite fabricator. Her badge says AMARA OBI, P3 — COMPOSITE ASSEMBLY, and her face says something less administrative.
1497|
1498|"Dr. Okafor," she says. She does not salute. The orbital workforce does not stand on ceremony, but the omission is deliberate, and they both know it.
1499|
1500|"Ms. Obi."

{"content": "1501|
1502|"We're not working."
1503|
1504|Okafor looks past her at the sixty workers behind her. Some meet his eyes. Some look at the floor. One man — young, maybe twenty-five, with the thin frame that comes from a year of reduced rations in microgravity — is holding a tablet displaying a number: 28,417. Okafor recognizes it immediately. It is the number of people selected as colonists for Platform 3's assigned ships. Twenty-eight thousand four hundred and seventeen will leave. Eight billion will not.
1505|
1506|"I see that," Okafor says. "Can you tell me why?"
1507|
1508|"We're building ships for other people," Amara says. Her voice is level. She has rehearsed this. "People who were selected. People with the right genes. We are building the vehicles that will carry them to safety while we die here. And we want to know why we are doing that."
1509|
1510|The gallery is quiet. Through the observation ports, the construction bays are visible — scaffolding, cranes, half-assembled trusses floating in the neutral buoyancy of microgravity. The bays are empty of workers. The work has stopped.
1511|
1512|"You are doing it," Okafor says carefully, "because without these ships, there is no future for anyone. The colony fails. The species ends."
1513|
1514|"The selected people's version of the species ends," Amara says. "Our version doesn't have a version. That's the point."
1515|
1516|Okafor nods. He does not argue the logic because the logic is sound. The Selection Committee's criteria are based on genetic markers — Pres1 mutation absence, telomere length, immune system diversity, psychological resilience scoring. The colonists are not chosen because they are better. They are chosen because their biology gives the colony the highest probability of survival. Okafor understands this. He also understands that understanding is not the same as acceptance, and acceptance is not the same as the willingness to build your own coffin.
1517|
1518|"You have demands," Okafor says. It is not a question.
1519|
1520|Amara pulls up a document on her tablet and transmits it to his wrist display. He reads it in twelve seconds.
1521|
1522|*One: Expand the colonist pool by 15,000 berths, allocated to current orbital construction personnel and their immediate families.*
1523|
1524|*Two: If berth expansion is not feasible, freeze all construction until the Selection Committee reviews the exclusion criteria Priority D and Priority E workers.*
1525|
1526|*Three: Public release of the Selection Committee's full scoring methodology.*
1527|
1528|Okafor reads it twice. He looks at Amara. "Fifteen thousand berths."
1529|
1530|"Fifteen thousand people will die so that someone else's genetic profile can survive. We're not asking for all of us. We're asking for a chance."
1531|
1532|Okafor does the math. It is the math he always does, the math that lives in his body like a second pulse. Fifteen thousand additional berths means fifteen additional ships, given the current pod configuration of sixteen pods per hibernation module. Fifteen ships means fifteen sets of trusses, sails, canisters, crew spheres, and systems buses. Fifteen ships means twenty-four thousand additional components, each manufactured to tolerances measured in microns, each assembled by workers who are already operating at the edge of capacity. The launch window closes in thirty-seven days.
1533|
1534|"You know I can't authorize fifteen thousand berths," he says.
1535|
1536|"No," Amara says. "We know you can't authorize anything. We know you're going to take this to the people who can. And we know that while you're talking, the ships don't get built. That's the leverage. It's the only leverage we have."
1537|
1538|Okafor believes her. Not because she is right about the leverage — she is — but because she is transparent about it. She is not disguised as a protester or a revolutionary or a martyr. She is a composite fabricator who has spent eight months layering carbon fiber onto keel trusses, and she is tired, and she is afraid, and she is asking for something she knows she will not get.
1539|
1540|He opens a channel to Houston. The encrypted link takes six seconds to establish. The person on the other end is Catherine Wu — no relation to Jennifer, a fact that Okafor has confirmed three times — the Interim Governance Bureau's deputy director for workforce operations. Okafor summarizes the situation in forty seconds.
1541|
1542|"How many workers?" Catherine asks.
1543|
1544|"Sixty-one confirmed. Could grow."
1545|
1546|"Demands?"
1547|
1548|He transmits the document. She reads it in silence. He can hear her breathing through the encrypted channel — slow, measured, the rhythm of a person doing her own math.
1549|
1550|"Fifteen thousand is impossible," she says. "The ships don't exist."
1551|
1552|"Then we need an alternative."
1553|
1554|"The alternative is they stop working and we miss the launch window and nobody goes anywhere."
1555|
1556|"Yes."
1557|
1558|Catherine is quiet for three seconds. Then: "I'm sending you a workforce contingency file. Negotiate from that. And David — buy me time. I need to talk to the Selection Committee."
1559|
1560|The channel closes. The file arrives on his wrist display. Okafor reads it standing in the gallery with sixty-one people watching him, and he finds the paragraph he needs on the third page.
1561|
1562|He looks at Amara.
1563|
1564|"I can't expand the colonist pool. The ships are already built or in final assembly. Adding fifteen thousand berths means building fifteen more ships, and we don't have the time, the materials, or the capacity."
1565|
1566|"I know."
1567|
1568|"But I can offer you something else."
1569|
1570|He transmits the paragraph to her tablet. She reads it. Her expression does not change.
1571|
1572|"The maintenance crew," she says.
1573|
1574|"Every ship requires a ten-person maintenance team during the cruise phase. These are not colonist positions — the crew sphere accommodates them. They wake from hibernation at designated intervals to perform inspections, repairs, system checks. They are not colonists. They are passengers. They travel. They survive. They arrive."
1575|
1576|"How many positions?"
1577|
1578|"Sixty ships. Ten maintenance per ship. Six hundred. It's not fifteen thousand. It's not even close. But it's six hundred people who would otherwise stay behind, and it's me offering it to you right now, with authorization from the Bureau contingent on work resuming within the hour."
1579|
1580|Amara reads the document again. Behind her, some of the workers are reading it on their own tablets, transmitted through the mesh network. Okafor can see them processing the number — six hundred out of how many? The orbital workforce numbers approximately twelve thousand across all platforms. Six hundred is five percent. It is a door cracked open six inches.
1581|
1582|"It's not enough," Amara says.
1583|
1584|"I know it's not enough. It's what exists."
1585|
1586|The silence stretches for eight seconds. Then the young man with the thin frame — the one who was holding the tablet with the number 28,417 — says, quietly, "I'll take it."
1587|
1588|Another voice, from the back: "I'll take it."
1589|
1590|Amara turns. "You don't speak for everyone."
1591|
1592|"I'm speaking for me."
1593|
1594|More voices. Not all of them. Maybe half. Thirty, thirty-five workers nodding, raising hands, pulling up the acceptance form on their tablets. The others remain still. Amara looks at Okafor with an expression he cannot read — not anger, not defeat, something more complicated, something that belongs to a person who has just watched her coalition fracture along the seam between pragmatism and principle.
1595|
1596|"Two days," Okafor says. "The work stoppage cost us two days. We don't have two days."
1597|
1598|"Some of us know that," Amara says.
1599|
1600|She transmits her acceptance of the maintenance crew offer at 0702. Thirty-seven workers follow her. Twenty-four do not. They remain in the docking gallery for another eleven minutes before dispersing to their quarters. They do not return to work.
1601|
1602|Okafor reports the numbers to Catherine. She acknowledges. The twenty-four are flagged for reassignment to non-critical tasks. They will not work on the ships again. There is no punishment — the Lightship program does not have a disciplinary architecture complex enough for this — but there is a kind of gravity to the decision, an inflection point that settles into the program's history like a weld seam: the moment when the people who built the future decided they wanted to be part of it.
1603|
1604|Within two hours, the bays on Platform 3 are full again. The cranes move. The riggers float. The welders fire their torches at carbon-fiber joints, and the sparks drift in microgravity like slow orange stars.
1605|
1606|The work continues. But it continues differently now, with an awareness that was not there before — the knowledge that the ships are not just engineering. They are argument. They are answer. They are the visible, physical shape of a choice that someone made about who deserves to survive, and the people who build them are not machines. They are hands, and hands have opinions about what they build.
1607|
1608|David Okafor spends the rest of the day on the phones — Houston, Geneva, the Selection Committee's emergency session — managing the fallout and the negotiations and the slow, grinding work of holding a coalition together with six hundred berths and thirty-seven minutes of compromise.
1609|
1610|At 2200, he is back in the transit capsule, returning to Platform 1, and he observes the construction bays through the capsule's viewport. The ships hang in their cradles like needles, like questions, like the only answer humanity has managed to produce.
1611|
1612|He thinks about Amara Obi, who accepted a maintenance position for Ship 14 because five percent was better than zero percent. He thinks about the twenty-four who did not accept, who returned to their quarters and closed their hatchways and made a different choice.
1613|
1614|He thinks about the twenty-eight thousand four hundred and seventeen who were selected, and the eight billion who were not, and the fact that the entire program — sixty ships, four-kilometer sails, seven thousand two hundred laser modules, a hundred and twenty years of transit, the fate of a species — depends on the willingness of twelve thousand workers to build what they will not ride.
1615|
1616|The capsule docks. Okafor pulls himself through the airlock and into Platform 1's corridor, where the lights are dimmed for the night cycle and the only sound is the hum of the ventilation system.
1617|
1618|He has fourteen hours before the next crisis. He intends to sleep for six of them.
1619|
1620|The work continues.
1621|# Chapter 17: Hibernation Training
1622|
1623|![](chapter_images/ch14.png)
1624|
1625|Sarah Brennan has trained astronauts for eleven years, and she has never had to explain to a group of them that thirty percent of them will die.
1626|
1627|She is standing at the front of Training Hall B at the Houston facility — a converted aircraft hangar with rows of reclining chairs, monitoring equipment, and a wall of screens displaying biometric data in real time — facing forty-eight people who have been selected as colonists for Ships 14 through 17. They are engineers, biologists, agronomists, physicians, three teachers, a veterinarian, a carpenter who cried when he received his selection letter, and a twenty-six-year-old geologist named Tomás Reyes who has been awake for thirty-six hours because he could not sleep knowing that in six weeks he will go to sleep and not wake up for a hundred and twenty years.
1628|
1629|"I'll be direct with you," Sarah says. "That's the only way I know how to do this."
1630|
1631|The hall is quiet. The forty-eight are seated in six rows of eight. They have been in the training program for four days. They have received orientations, facility tours, mission briefings, and a nutrition plan designed to optimize their body composition for hibernation induction. They have not received the talk. This is the talk.
1632|
1633|"The hibernation process takes two weeks from initiation to pod-sealing," Sarah begins. "I'm going to walk you through every phase, and then I'm going to tell you the number. And then I'm going to answer your questions. And then I'm going to tell you the number again, because once is never enough."
1634|
1635|She taps her tablet. The wall screen displays a metabolic curve — a human metabolism declining over fourteen days from normal function to twelve percent of baseline.
1636|
1637|"We initiate with a metabolic reduction protocol. You'll receive a series of drugs — synthetic hibernation inducers, developed over the past eight years from research into mammalian torpor. The first dose is administered on Day One. It slows your heart rate, reduces your core temperature, and begins the process of shifting your body from normal metabolic function to a state of controlled hypothermia. Your temperature drops one degree every forty-eight hours. Brain activity diminishes but does not cease. You will drift in and out of consciousness for the first week. The medical team monitors you continuously."
1638|
1639|She advances the slide. A diagram of a hibernation pod appears — a cylindrical capsule lined with sensors, intravenous lines, cooling elements, and a waste management system that she chooses not to describe in detail.
1640|
1641|"By Day Seven, your core temperature reaches eighteen degrees Celsius. By Day Ten, it reaches eight. By Day Twelve, it stabilizes at four degrees. At this point, your body is consuming one-twelfth of its normal energy. Your heart beats once every forty seconds. Your brain activity is detectable but minimal. Ship Three suffered a catastrophic sail deployment failure during testing — the membrane tore along a seam that passed quality inspection because the inspection standard was written by people who were running out of time. Ship Seven experienced a hibernation pod cascade failure six months into the shakedown — a software error in the thermal regulation system that was corrected on all subsequent ships, but only after three hundred and ten people stopped breathing. We carry those losses. They are part of the weight."
1964|
1965|He leans forward slightly.
1966|
1967|"The array is seventy-two percent complete. This number will not change in the next thirty days. We will not add the remaining twenty-eight percent of modules. We can't. The manufacturing facilities on Earth are offline — ice, infrastructure collapse, the slow death of the world that built you. The seventy-two percent we have is enough. The math is clear. One hundred and sixty-eight modules, each delivering six hundred and forty megawatts, focused through a phased array to produce a coherent beam that will strike sails four kilometers across at a range of up to twelve light-minutes. The ships will accelerate at one point seven meters per second squared for one hundred and seventy-four days. They will reach four point two percent of the speed of light. They will coast for one hundred and eighteen years. The math is clear."
1968|
1969|He says this like a prayer. Like if he says it enough times, it will stay true.
1970|
1971|"The math is also clear about survival rates. Seventy percent. Seventy percent of colonists will survive the transit. This means that of the seventeen thousand four hundred and twenty who sleep aboard these ships, approximately five thousand two hundred and twenty-six will not wake up. Their pods will fail. Their bodies will warm. They will die in the dark between stars, and no one will know, and no one will mourn them, because everyone they have ever known will also be dead or sleeping."
1972|
1973|He takes a breath.
1974|
1975|"I tell you this because you deserve the truth. You have always deserved the truth. We have not always given it to you, and I am sorry for that. The Exodus has been built on urgency and desperation and the mathematical certainty that staying means dying. It has also been built on hope — irrational, irrational hope that a beam of light and a sheet of engineered polymer and a billion frozen human beings can cross the void between worlds and plant a seed."
1976|
1977|His voice catches. He steadies it.
1978|
1979|"The Earth is frozen. The last transmission from the United Nations headquarters in Geneva came eighteen days ago through two meters of accumulated snow and the last functioning deep-repeat fiber node. The UN is still operational. Forty-three nations are still technically represented. The population of Earth is estimated at four hundred million, down from eleven billion, and falling. The fusion plants in Siberia and Patagonia are still online. The ones in North America are not. The ice sheets have reached the forty-fifth parallel in the Northern Hemisphere and the fortieth in the Southern. London is buried. Beijing is buried. Montreal has been under ice for eleven years."
1980|
1981|He pauses.
1982|
1983|"We cannot save them. We can only save you. And in thirty days, that is exactly what we will do."
1984|
1985|He reaches forward and stops the recording. The red light goes dark. David sits in the cold studio for a long time, his hands on the console, his breath visible in the thin heating of the module.
1986|
1987|Then he uploads the message to the primary communication array and routes it to all fifty-eight ships.
1988|
1989|It takes four minutes to transmit because the signal must be boosted through three relay satellites, two of which are running on emergency power. The message arrives at each ship in a compressed data packet tagged PRIORITY ALPHA — the highest classification in the Exodus communication protocol, reserved for directives from the Director of Operations.
1990|
1991|On Ship 17, *Catalyst*, the communications officer opens the file and watches it on a monitor in the operations bay. She is the only crew member not in hibernation — part of the rotating watch, three months awake, then sleep, then wake at destination. She watches David Okafor deliver his message to the seventeen thousand four hundred and twenty people frozen in the bays behind her, and she feels the weight of it settle on her chest like a physical thing.
1992|
1993|She thinks about Ship 3. She knew people on Ship 3.
1994|
1995|She thinks about the seventy percent.
1996|
1997|She sends the message to the ship's archive, flagged for automatic playback to every hibernation pod upon arrival. In one hundred and eighteen years, the colonists of *Catalyst* will wake, and the first thing they will hear will be David Okafor's voice, telling them how many of them didn't make it.
1998|
1999|On all fifty-eight ships, the same sequence plays out. The message arrives. It is archived. It is tagged for playback on arrival. The colonists sleep on, unaware, their dreams silenced at minus 196 degrees.
