{"content": "3001|On Earth, in Lagos, a man named Obi Nwosu steps out of his apartment onto the concrete landing outside his door. It is early evening here, the sun having set twenty minutes ago, the sky that particular shade of deep indigo that comes just after twilight but before true dark. He is not thinking about the fleet. He is thinking about dinner, and about his daughter's school project, and about the pothole on Cemetery Road that the municipal council keeps promising to fix.
3002|
3003|Then he looks up and sees a star that was not there before.
3004|
3005|Brighter than Venus. Brighter than anything in the sky except the Moon itself, and positioned near the Moon, a cluster of points that are unmistakably not fixed, not steady, not the calm unwavering lights of distant suns. These are moving. Slowly, but visibly — he can see them shifting against the background of constellations, each one a tiny fierce point climbing.
3006|
3007|His hands are shaking. He does not know why. He is not an engineer or a scientist. He works at a textile import company and follows the news with the casual interest of someone who knows that some events are too large to engage with seriously. But he knows what this is. Everyone knows what this is. The feed has been explaining it for months, for years — fifty-eight lightships, departing the solar system, carrying 580,000 colonists to Proxima Centauri.
3008|
3009|Fifty-eight new stars, climbing into the sky.
3010|
3011|His daughter appears behind him in the doorway. She is seven. She asks what they are. He tells her they are ships. She asks where they are going. He tells her very far away. She asks if people are inside. He tells her yes, 580,000 people, and her eyes widen.
3012|
3013|Up above them, the sails continue to glow. The acceleration climbs. Ship One is now moving at eleven kilometers per second and gaining speed with every passing minute. The formation holds — 58 precise circles of light, arranged in three staggered columns like a fleet review on the ocean of space, each ship maintaining its position to within a hundred meters of its assigned coordinate through constant micro-adjustments of sail angle.
3014|
3015|The beam sustains.
3016|
3017|---
3018|
3019|Back in Mission Control, Patricia breaks the silence. Her voice is calm, professional, carrying through the room with the practiced clarity of someone who has spent years learning to speak into microphones under pressure.
3020|
3021|"All ships nominal. Beam delivery within point-zero-three percent of target parameters. Acceleration curves on track across the board. No anomalies reported from any deployment monitor." She pauses. Looks at the main screen, where 58 green indicators burn steady and bright. "We are underway."
3022|
3023|The room does not erupt. There is no cheering, no champagne, no embraces. These are people who have been working for eighteen hours straight and who know that the next 4.24 light-years will present problems that no one has yet imagined. What there is, instead, is a collective exhalation — a release of tension so pervasive and so quiet that it is almost its own kind of silence.
3024|
3025|Dr. Maya Okonkwo puts her hand on Patricia's shoulder. Says nothing. The gesture contains everything.
3026|
3027|In Mombasa, in Calgary, in São Paulo and Dhaka and Sapporo and Reykjavik, millions look up. Social media feeds saturate with blurry photographs of points of light near the Moon. News anchors try to maintain their composure and mostly fail. A child in rural Montana points at the sky and tells her mother that the stars are running away, and her mother, who has read the briefings extensively, says yes, honey, they are, and if she is not entirely sure whether she means the stars or the people aboard them, the distinction does not seem to matter.
3028|
3029|The sails glow. The beam holds. Fifty-eight ships, each carrying ten thousand souls in cryogenic suspension, each piloted by a skeleton crew of twelve awake engineers and caretakers, begin the long slow acceleration that will, over the coming weeks, push them to cruising speed.
3030|
3031|The age of lightships has begun.
3032|# Chapter 31: Sail Deployment
3033|
3034|![](chapter_images/ch28.png)
3035|
3036|Patricia Okonkwo has been awake for nineteen hours and she can feel every one of them in the base of her skull, a dull pressure that pulses in time with her heartbeat. The caffeine has stopped working. She drinks another cup anyway, because the ritual matters.
3037|
3038|It is hour one of sail deployment, and the first five ships go nominal.
3039|
3040|Ship One's sail reaches full deployment at T plus forty-seven minutes. The telemetry confirms it across eleven independent sensor arrays — laser interferometry, thermal imaging, reflected-light photography from the ship's own inspection drones. The membrane is a perfect circle, four kilometers edge to edge, tensioned to within one percent of target spec.
3041|
3042|Patricia signs the confirmation. Her stylus is steady.
3043|
3044|Ship Two deploys at T plus fifty-one minutes. Ship Four at T plus fifty-eight minutes. Ship Nine at T plus sixty-three minutes.
3045|
3046|The numbers accumulate. Patricia watches the deployment queue cascade through her console, each ship's sail unfurling like a flower in time-lapse — except the timescale is minutes and the petals are membranes thin enough that individual air molecules could punch through them like bullets if oriented wrong. But they are oriented right.
3047|
3048|Then Ship Fourteen's feed goes amber.
3049|
3050|"Rib Seventeen is lagging," says Wei Tan from the adjacent console. "Three-second delay on the extension actuator. Temperature spike at the hub joint."
3051|
3052|Patricia pulls up the diagnostic. The deployment mechanism — a carbon-composite rib system designed to unfold the sail from its storage canister — is showing asymmetric extension. Rib Seventeen is three degrees behind its paired counterpart, Rib Eighteen. The membrane is developing a stress gradient.
3053|
3054|"Hold deployment. Engage the tension compensation system."
3055|
3056|The compensation system is a backup — a set of micro-actuators embedded in the sail's edge that can apply differential tension to correct minor asymmetries. Patricia watches the telemetry as the system engages. The stress gradient flattens. Rib Seventeen catches up.
3057|
3058|But the temperature at the hub joint continues rising.
3059|
3060|"Two hundred and seventy Kelvin," Tan reports. "Two eighty-five. Three hundred."
3061|
3062|The maximum rating for the hub joint is three hundred and eighty Kelvin before the carbon composite begins to degrade. They have margin. But the rate of increase is wrong — three degrees per second, sustained.
3063|
3064|"Abort deployment on Ship Fourteen," Patricia says. "Retract and inspect."
3065|
3066|"I need authorization —"
3067|
3068|"You have it. Abort now."
3069|
3070|The retraction sequence begins. The sail membrane folds back into its canister, guided by the same micro-actuators that deployed it. Patricia watches the hub joint temperature plateau at three hundred and twenty Kelvin, then begin to drop.
3071|
3072|The fleet master log shows: SHIP 14 — DEPLOYMENT ABORTED. HUB JOINT THERMAL ANOMALY. INVESTIGATION IN PROGRESS.
3073|
3074|Patricia stares at the entry. Fourteen ships deployed successfully. One aborted. Each abort means a delay. Each delay means a ship that might not launch before the ice closes the launch window.
3075|
3076|On the main screen, Ship Twenty-One's sail begins its deployment sequence. Ship Thirty-Three follows. The work continues.
3077|
3078|Ship Twenty-One deploys cleanly in sixty-two minutes. Ship Thirty-Three takes seventy-one but completes nominal. Ship Forty-One has a minor tension fluctuation that the compensation system corrects in fourteen seconds.
3079|
3080|And Ship Fifty-Two — the ship that Jennifer Wu tried to sabotage, the one she ultimately spared — deploys flawlessly. Patricia signs the confirmation. Her hand does not tremble.
3081|
3082|---
3083|
3084|Ship Forty.
3085|
3086|The number catches Patricia's attention. The ship that almost was not a ship at all.
3087|
3088|Ship Forty's sail begins its unfurling sequence at T plus seventy-one minutes and twelve seconds. Rib One extends. Rib Two extends. The membrane begins its careful, breathtaking expansion from the hub outward, a circle growing in the void like the ripple from a stone dropped in still water — except the medium is not water but a fifty-nanometer membrane catching 144.8 gigawatts of laser light.
3089|
3090|Rib Twelve extends. Rib Nineteen extends. The membrane tensions.
3091|
3092|And then Rib Twenty-Seven freezes.
3093|
3094|Patricia sees it happen in the telemetry — the extension actuator on Rib Twenty-Seven hits full extension and keeps drawing current. The motor is stalled. The control system is trying to force the rib past its mechanical stop.
3095|
3096|"Emergency shutoff on Rib Twenty-Seven. Cut power to that actuator now."
3097|
3098|Tan's fingers fly across the console. The current draw spikes, then drops to zero as the emergency cutoff engages.
3099|
3100|The sail is now asymmetric. Twenty-six ribs fully deployed. One rib stalled at ninety-four percent. The membrane is pulling unevenly, creating a stress concentration at the stalled rib's attachment point.
3101|
3102|"Can we compensate?"
3103|
3104|Tan runs the numbers. "The tension system can correct for up to twelve percent asymmetry. We're at six. But the correction will put strain on Rigging Cable Four. It's rated for... this is within spec. Barely."
3105|
3106|"Do it."
3107|
3108|The tension compensation system engages. Patricia watches the stress distribution rebalance across the sail surface. The membrane smooths. The asymmetric pull on the stalled rib decreases.
3109|
3110|"Rib Twenty-Seven is still stuck," Tan says. "We'll need a spacewalk to clear the actuator."
3111|
3112|"How long?"
3113|
3114|"Four hours minimum. Six if the debris environment is active."
3115|
3116|Six hours. Patricia checks the launch window. The beam ignition sequence is scheduled for T plus twelve hours. If they delay deployment, the entire fleet's launch sequence shifts. Every other ship waits for Ship Forty.
3117|
3118|She makes the decision. "We deploy Ship Forty-one and Forty-three on schedule. Ship Forty gets the spacewalk team. Priority override on all platform maintenance requests — I want the best EVA crew available."
3119|
3120|The spacewalk team is assembled in thirty minutes. Patricia watches through the station's external cameras as two technicians in pressurized suits push off from the airlock and drift toward Ship Forty's deployment canister. The stalled actuator is visible as a dark spot against the reflective sail — a mechanical joint that refused to complete its final three degrees of rotation.
3121|
3122|The first technician reaches the canister and attaches her tether. Her voice comes through the comm: "I see the problem. The actuator housing has a burr on the drive shaft. Probably a manufacturing defect. I can file it down, but I'll need to disassemble the housing to get clearance."
3123|
3124|"How long?"
3125|
3126|"Two hours. Maybe three."
3127|
3128|"Do it."
3129|
3130|Patricia watches the clock. Three hours for the repair. One hour for re-inspection. The deployment window for Ship Forty closes at T plus nine hours. They have margin. Barely.
3131|
3132|At T plus seven hours and forty-one minutes, the technician finishes the repair. The actuator cycles freely. Ship Forty's sail deploys to full extension in forty-seven minutes. Eleven sensor arrays confirm nominal. Reflected light patterns match models to four decimal places.
3133|
3134|One hundred and sixty-five green indicators.
3135|
3136|Patricia signs the confirmation. Her stylus traces the signature with the same steadiness she has applied to every other.
3137|
3138|The deployment continues. Ship Fifty-Eight deploys cleanly. Fifty-eight circles of metamaterial membrane, four kilometers across, catching light that has been traveling since it left the lunar array's focusing optics.
3139|
3140|It is, Patricia thinks, the most beautiful thing she has ever seen. Not the sails themselves — though they are beautiful, each one a mirror made of almost nothing. What is beautiful is the togetherness of it. The way 120,000 people who disagreed about everything produced, through years of argument and compromise and sheer stubborn work, something that functions. Something that deploys. Something that works.
3141|
3142|"All sails deployed. All confirmations signed."
3143|
3144|She sets the stylus down. Closes the deployment file. Opens the acceleration monitoring queue, because the ships need to reach cruising speed and there is a narrow window for course corrections and the work is not done.
3145|
3146|It is never done. This is what she has learned in fourteen years of building impossible things: the work is never done. It merely transitions into new forms, new problems, new signatures required.
3147|
3148|Patricia's hands are steady.
3149|
3150|# Chapter 32: The Acceleration
3151|
3152|The acceleration is barely perceptible.
3153|
3154|Robert Okonkwo feels it as a faint heaviness in his limbs, a subtle shift in the way his coffee sits in its cup, as though the liquid has decided to press harder against the ceramic floor. 0.03 g. Thirty milligravities. A fraction of what the Moon's surface gravity already denies him. If he did not know it was happening — if the instruments did not confirm it with their relentless precision — he would have no way of knowing that the machine he spent forty years building is currently firing, that 7,200 laser modules on the surface above and around him are pouring 461 terawatts of coherent light into a column of photons aimed at fifty-eight sails, each sail pushing a ship carrying ten thousand human beings toward a star.
3155|
3156|He knows. The instruments make sure of that.
3157|
3158|But the feeling is nothing. The feeling is less than the memory of Earth gravity, which he has not felt in four decades and which exists now only as a ghost in his muscles, a phantom weight that sometimes wakes him in the night. The acceleration is a whisper. A suggestion. A nuance in the way things settle.
3159|
3160|It is enough. It has to be enough. It is, according to the mathematics that Robert has carried in his head since before most of the wake crew were born, the beginning of everything.
3161|
3162|---
3163|
3164|Day 1.
3165|
3166|The wake crews go through their routines the way surgeons go through pre-op checklists — not because they do not know the steps, but because the steps are the structure that keeps the mind from wandering into the territory of what could go wrong.
3167|
3168|Life support first. On every ship, the awake crew cycles through the atmospheric monitoring panels: oxygen partial pressure, carbon dioxide scrubber efficiency, trace contaminant levels, humidity, temperature. The numbers are green. They have been green since the pods sealed. They will stay green for one hundred and twenty years if the systems hold, and the systems were built to hold, and the crews are awake specifically to make sure that holding continues.
3169|
3170|Hibernation pod status second. Ten thousand pods per ship. Fifty-eight ships. Five hundred and eighty thousand people in chemical suspension, their metabolisms slowed to a crawl, their body temperatures held at four degrees above freezing, their brains quieted to a state so close to death that the difference is measured in the presence of a few carefully maintained ion gradients that wake the neurons when the time comes. If the time comes.
3171|
3172|The pod telemetry scrolls across the screens in waves of data: cardiac rhythm flatline-slow, one beat per minute. Brain activity suppressed but present, a whisper of delta waves in an ocean of chemical silence. Core temperature stable. Cryoprotectant concentration nominal. Each pod a closed system, a sealed world, a person reduced to a set of numbers that mean alive, alive, alive.
3173|
3174|The crews check them anyway. They check them every four hours. They will check them for the three days they remain awake, until the beam cuts and the ships are on their way and the crews climb into their own pods to sleep the long sleep and let the machines mind the machines.
3175|
3176|Sail alignment third. This is where the mathematics lives. The sail — four kilometers of carbon-composite membrane, fifty nanometers thick, tensioned between deployable ribs like the skin of a drum — must maintain its angle relative to the beam to within a fraction of a degree. Too much tilt and the reflected photons push the ship off course. Too little and the beam overcorrects. The sail is a rudder and an engine simultaneously, and its angle is the only thing between a ship that arrives at Lacaille 9352 and a ship that sails past it into the void.
3177|
3178|The crews watch the alignment telemetry the way parents watch a sleeping child's chest: obsessively, lovingly, with a desperate attention to the rhythm of rising and falling, holding and releasing.
3179|
3180|---
3181|
3182|The Moon's array tracks each ship independently.
3183|
3184|This is the part that Robert thinks about when the quiet moments come — and they do come, because the acceleration is steady and the machines are reliable and the hours between checklists are filled with the kind of silence that makes a mind wander. The array does not fire a single beam that all ships share. It fires 7,200 individual beams, each one phase-locked to its neighbors but aimed at its own target, each one riding a ship's sail like a spotlight tracking a performer across a stage.
3185|
3186|And the ships are moving. They are 140,000 miles from the Moon at the start of the burn and climbing, their distance increasing with every second, the beam spreading slightly as it travels, the array's focusing optics compensating in real time — adjusting the phase relationships between modules to keep the beam tight, to keep the power density constant, to keep the sail loaded within its design parameters.
3187|
3188|Robert watches from Station One, where the main display shows the 7,200 modules arranged in a topographic map of Mare Imbrium. Each module is a point of light. Most are green — green for nominal, green for firing, green for holding. A few pulse amber as their thermal management systems cycle, heating and cooling the amplifier rods to maintain the precise temperature differential that keeps the frequency lock stable. This is expected. The amber is not alarm. The amber is breathing. The machine breathes, and the breath shows as color on the screen.
3189|
3190|His modules. His array. Forty years of his life spread across sixty-three kilometers of lunar regolith, and it is holding.
3191|
3192|Robert Kanake sits at the console to his left, monitoring the phase-lock coherence across the array. Emily Park is on the far side of the room, tracking the beam director alignment. The others — six engineers and technicians, the core of the fire team — occupy their stations with the quiet focus of people who understand that the number they are watching represents the velocity of five hundred and eighty thousand lives.
3193|

3662|The sails are intact—all fifty-eight of them, each one a mirror of aluminum and carbon nanotube composite, a kilometer across, thinner than a human hair, catching the light of a distant laser and converting it into motion. They have been struck by micrometeorites, degraded by cosmic radiation, stressed by thermal cycling and sail reorientations and the slow, patient accumulation of a century in space. But they hold. The engineers who built them gave them margins—safety factors of four on the rigging, six on the sail material, eight on the structural members. The margins have been tested. They have held.
3663|
3664|The hibernation pods show green.
3665|
3666|Twelve thousand, one hundred and eighty people are dreaming of a new world. They are agronomists and neurologists and structural engineers and teachers and children who were born on Earth and will grow up on a planet orbiting a star that their parents chose for them. They are the last generation to remember the Sun as anything other than a bright star, and the first generation to see Proxima Centauri as anything other than a red smudge in a telescope. They are the bridge between two worlds, and they are sleeping through the crossing, trusting the ships and the sails and the wake crews to carry them safely to the other side.
3667|
3668|The fleet's communication network—a mesh of tight-beam laser links connecting all fifty-eight ships—carries a constant stream of data. System status reports. Sail alignment updates. Hibernation pod telemetry. And, between the official traffic, the personal messages. Wake crew to wake crew, ship to ship, a conversation that has been running for a hundred and twenty years without interruption. They share recipes and music and arguments about politics that no longer exist on a planet that no longer matters. They share jokes about the food paste that sustains them during their waking rotations. They share photographs of the stars as seen from different ships, different angles, different moments in the long transit. They share, above all, the knowledge that they are not alone.
3669|
3670|Ship 23's current wake crew is Captain Tomás Reyes and his three engineers. Tomás is on his second rotation. He has read every log entry that Michael Torres wrote during his seven rotations, and he has read the entries of every captain who held the chair before and after. He knows the ship's history the way a priest knows scripture—not as abstract knowledge but as lived experience, a chain of human attention stretching back to the day the ship left the Solar System.
3671|
3672|On this particular day, Tomás sits in the captain's chair and opens a channel to the fleet.
3673|
3674|"Ship 23 to all ships. Day forty-three of this rotation. All systems nominal. All three hundred and ten colonists in stasis, no anomalies. Sail alignment optimal. Laser coupling efficiency at ninety-seven point one percent. We are currently traveling at fourteen point eight kilometers per second. Deceleration phase in approximately four years and two months." He pauses. "The stars look good today. Ship 23 out."
3675|
3676|The responses come in over the next few minutes, ship by ship, a roll call of the fleet. Ship 7 confirms. Ship 12 confirms. Ship 19 confirms. Ship 31 confirms. Ship 35 confirms. All fifty-eight ships, one by one, each voice saying the same thing in different words: we are here, we are holding, we are coming.
3677|
3678|The Age of Lightships has begun.
3679|
3680|Not with a declaration or a ceremony or a moment of triumph. 3681|
3682|Behind them, the Sun dims. Ahead of them, Proxima brightens. Between the two, fifty-eight ships carry twelve thousand dreams through the dark.

function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

cross_profile.description: Opt out of the cross-profile soft guard. Defaults to false. Set true ONLY after explicit user direction to edit another Hermes profile's skills/plugins/cron/memories.

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — bg without notify runs SILENTLY and you have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself. Two legitimate uses:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — silent is correct, there's no exit to notify on.
  (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — MUST set notify_on_complete=true. Without it you'll either forget to poll or sit blocked waiting for the user to surface the result.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — without it, the process runs silently and you'll have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself (easy to forget, leading to silent blindness on long jobs). Two legitimate patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — these stay silent because there's no exit to notify on. (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — these MUST set notify_on_complete=true. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits. Auto-runs syntax checks on .py/.json/.yaml/.toml and other linted languages; only NEW errors introduced by this write are surfaced (pre-existing errors are filtered out).

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

cross_profile.description: Opt out of the cross-profile soft guard. Defaults to false. Set true ONLY after explicit user direction to edit another Hermes profile's skills/plugins/cron/memories — by default these writes are blocked with a warning because they affect a different profile than the one this session is running under.
